1.summary: Paul thanks God for the Philippians' partnership in the gospel, prays their love will abound, reports that his imprisonment has advanced the gospel, and weighs life and death, concluding that to live is Christ and to die is gain; he urges them to stand together worthy of the gospel.
1.lookfor: Notice how Paul reads his own situation, and his attitude to rivals preaching Christ.

names.name: Timothy
names.gloss: Paul's co-worker, well known to the Philippians.

names.name: Philippi
names.gloss: A Roman colony in Macedonia, northern Greece.

insights.title: Partnership
insights.body: Paul thanks God for their partnership, koinonia, in the gospel from the first day (1:5). They had supported him financially again and again.

insights.title: He who began a good work
insights.body: Paul is confident that he who began a good work in you will complete it until the day of Christ (1:6). God finishes what he starts.

insights.title: The praetorian guard
insights.body: Paul's chains became known throughout the whole praetorian guard (1:13), the emperor's elite soldiers. Guards chained to him in shifts became a captive audience.

insights.title: Rivals preaching Christ
insights.body: Some preach Christ out of envy, hoping to add to Paul's troubles. His answer: what does it matter? Christ is proclaimed, and I rejoice (1:15-18). The message mattered more than his reputation.

insights.title: To live is Christ
insights.body: To me to live is Christ, and to die is gain (1:21). Paul would rather depart and be with Christ, but staying is more needful for them (1:23-24).

insights.title: Citizens
insights.body: Let your manner of life be worthy of the gospel (1:27); the verb means live as citizens. Philippi was proud of its Roman citizenship; believers are citizens of a greater commonwealth.

insights.title: Reading your circumstances
insights.body: Paul saw his prison as a platform. What difficult circumstance of yours might God be using in ways you haven't noticed?

2.summary: Paul urges unity and humility, pointing to Christ, who emptied himself, became a servant, and died on a cross, and whom God exalted as Lord; he calls them to work out their salvation, shine like stars, and commends Timothy and Epaphroditus as examples.
2.lookfor: Notice the hymn in verses 6 to 11, with its downward and upward movement, and the real people who model it.

names.name: Timothy
names.gloss: Paul's genuine son in the faith, who cared for others' interests.

names.name: Epaphroditus
names.gloss: The Philippians' messenger, who nearly died serving Paul.

insights.title: Others first
insights.body: Do nothing through rivalry or conceit, but in humility count others more significant than yourselves; look to others' interests, not only your own (2:3-4).

insights.title: An early hymn
insights.body: Verses 6 to 11 read like a hymn or poem, possibly sung by the earliest Christians. It is one of the oldest statements about who Jesus is.

insights.title: He emptied himself
insights.body: Christ, being in the form of God, didn't count equality with God something to be grasped, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant (2:6-7). He didn't stop being God; he poured himself out in service.

insights.title: Even death on a cross
insights.body: He humbled himself, becoming obedient to death, even the death of the cross (2:8). Roman citizens like the Philippians were exempt from crucifixion; it was the slave's death.

insights.title: Every knee shall bow
insights.body: At Jesus' name every knee should bow and every tongue confess that he is Lord (2:10-11). Isaiah said this of the Lord God alone; Paul applies it to Jesus.

insights.title: Work out, God works in
insights.body: Work out your own salvation with fear and trembling, for it is God who works in you (2:12-13). Our effort and God's work aren't rivals; his working makes ours possible.

insights.title: Shining like stars
insights.body: Shine as lights in the world, in a crooked and perverse generation (2:15), turning Moses' words about Israel into a calling for the church.

insights.title: The mind of Christ
insights.body: Paul says, have this mind in you which was also in Christ Jesus (2:5). Where could you take the lower place this week?

3.summary: Paul warns against those who demand circumcision, lists his own impressive credentials and counts them as loss compared with knowing Christ; he presses on toward the goal, and reminds them that their citizenship is in heaven.
3.lookfor: Notice Paul's balance sheet of gains and losses, and the runner's image.

names.name: Benjamin
names.gloss: Paul's tribe, which gave Israel its first king, Saul.

names.name: Pharisee
names.gloss: The party strictest about keeping the law.

insights.title: Beware of dogs
insights.body: Beware of the dogs, the evil workers, the false circumcision (3:2). Some Jews called Gentiles dogs; Paul turns the insult on those demanding circumcision.

insights.title: Paul's credentials
insights.body: Circumcised the eighth day, of Israel, of Benjamin, a Hebrew of Hebrews, a Pharisee, a zealous persecutor, blameless by the law's righteousness (3:5-6). If anyone could boast in the flesh, Paul could.

insights.title: Rubbish
insights.body: Paul counts everything as loss and as skubala (3:8), translated rubbish, refuse or even dung. Strong language for his own pedigree compared with knowing Christ.

insights.title: Righteousness from God
insights.body: Paul wants to be found in Christ, not having a righteousness of his own from the law, but the righteousness from God that comes through faith (3:9).

insights.title: Straining toward the goal
insights.body: Forgetting what lies behind and straining forward, I press on toward the goal for the prize (3:13-14). Paul pictures a runner leaning toward the finish, not looking back.

insights.title: Citizenship in heaven
insights.body: Our citizenship is in heaven, from which we await a Savior, who will transform our lowly body to be like his glorious body (3:20-21). Philippi's citizens looked to Rome; believers look to heaven.

insights.title: What you count as gain
insights.body: Paul's résumé became loss next to knowing Christ. What achievement or identity are you tempted to lean on?

4.summary: Paul urges two women to agree in the Lord, calls the church to rejoice always, not to be anxious but to pray with thanksgiving, and to think on what is true and lovely; he thanks them for their gift, having learned contentment in every situation through Christ who strengthens him.
4.lookfor: Notice the promise of peace after prayer, and the secret Paul learned about contentment.

names.name: Euodia
names.gloss: A woman who labored with Paul, at odds with Syntyche.

names.name: Syntyche
names.gloss: A co-worker of Paul, urged to agree with Euodia.

names.name: Clement
names.gloss: A fellow worker of Paul in Philippi.

names.name: Thessalonica
names.gloss: A city to which the Philippians sent Paul aid.

names.name: Epaphroditus
names.gloss: Who carried the Philippians' gift to Paul.

insights.title: Two women
insights.body: Paul pleads with Euodia and Syntyche to agree in the Lord (4:2). Both had labored with him in the gospel; their names are in the book of life, and their quarrel matters to the whole church.

insights.title: Rejoice always
insights.body: Rejoice in the Lord always; again I will say, rejoice (4:4). Written from prison, the command is not to feel happy but to find joy in the Lord whatever happens.

insights.title: Instead of anxiety
insights.body: Don't be anxious about anything, but in everything by prayer with thanksgiving let your requests be known to God (4:6). The result isn't guaranteed answers but God's peace guarding hearts.

insights.title: Guarding your hearts
insights.body: God's peace will guard your hearts and minds (4:7). The verb is military; Philippi was a garrison town settled by veteran soldiers.

insights.title: Content
insights.body: I have learned to be content in whatever state I am (4:11). The word autarkēs was Stoic, meaning self-sufficient; Paul redefines it as Christ-sufficient: I can do all things through Christ who strengthens me (4:13).

insights.title: A fragrant offering
insights.body: Paul calls their gift a sweet-smelling fragrance, an acceptable sacrifice (4:18), the language of Old Testament offerings. Giving to God's work is worship.

insights.title: Caesar's household
insights.body: All the saints greet you, especially those of Caesar's household (4:22): slaves and freedmen in the imperial service, the gospel reaching into the palace.

insights.title: Whatever is lovely
insights.body: Paul lists what to think about: true, honorable, just, pure, lovely, commendable (4:8). What fills your mind most, and how could you redirect it?

intro.who: Paul wrote it, with Timothy (1:1), to the church at Philippi, the first church he founded in Europe (Acts 16).
intro.when: About AD 60–62, from prison, most likely in Rome, though some suggest Ephesus or Caesarea. Paul didn't know whether he would live or die (1:20-24).
intro.why: To thank the Philippians for a gift sent with Epaphroditus, to update them on his imprisonment, to urge unity and humility modeled on Christ, and to warn against those who trusted in the flesh. Joy runs through the letter, written from chains.

outline.title: Joy in chains: to live is Christ
